what: terminal-revocation/0.1 opt-in section: presence makes a revoked (grant_id,revision) permanently refused (grant_revocation_recorded) even if status later reads active
owner_of_variation: Host builds RuntimeAuthorityProfile (terminal_revocation section); no Registry slot
narrowing_direction: off->on only (strictly more refusals); never on->off; absent/corrupt Registry input keeps host value
floor_in_code: Refusal logic and reason code stay in code; Registry could only force presence, never remove it; memory is the CP own record store (no keyed integrity, runtime_authority.py:184-186) so the floor of what it can remember stays in code
blocking_decision: Same open question as RG-C-010 and RG-C-009: how a Registry-forced profile section enters the profile dump / approval_commitment (section is exclude_if None for byte identity, runtime_authority.py:214). Also whether Registry-forced presence is meaningful when the host did not wire the section.
evidence: Row W8-013 retained as 'no tunable value', but the section is an optional safeguard whose only variation is on/off and whose consumer is a single check at bounded.py:2390. Exact parity with RG-C-010 (holder inventory required flag) and RG-C-020 (anchor_deadline_to_inputs) which the audit rates REGISTRY-ELIGIBLE as monotone bool tightening. Not in G0 current-candidate-ledger (no record names terminal revocation). Not a constitutional floor: it is opt-in today.

what: SyntheticRecoveryLedger writer_enabled constructor flag (False disables the append writer, recovery_resolution.py:236) bundled inside a RETAIN rule
owner_of_variation: Host deployment (process role wiring), same as revocation disposition_writer_enabled/closeout_writer_enabled
narrowing_direction: True->False only disables a writer (no widening)
floor_in_code: synthetic=True requirement and fail-closed default stay in code (recovery_resolution.py:96-97); profile is synthetic, production admission unsupported
blocking_decision: None for host-owned. If lead prefers, OUT-OF-SCOPE since the ledger is explicitly synthetic.
evidence: Sibling flags at revocation_closeout.py:91-92 are PROVIDER-OR-HOST-OWNED (NEW:revocation-writer-enable-flags, W3-073). Same operational meaning, same constructor-flag shape, different disposition. Add this site to that logical rule (parameter count unchanged, +1 site).

what: Selection anchor exclusive-lock wait LOCK_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=10.0 s (class constant), expiry raises anchor_lock_unavailable and writes nothing
owner_of_variation: Host operator (liveness tuning); Runtime code owns the fail-closed expiry
narrowing_direction: Longer or shorter wait only changes availability; expiry always refuses (no weakening direction)
floor_in_code: Fail-closed raise on expiry and the 'write nothing' behaviour stay in code
blocking_decision: Whether class-constant timeouts are worth exposing at all (no constructor argument today, so a host cannot set it without subclassing).
evidence: RG-B-022 retained as 'protected constant' list that lumps this wait with identifier regexes. The same kind of wait is rated host-owned in RG-B-018/019 (AuthorizationPinConfig.fence_deadline_seconds authorization_pin.py:52; InstallerConfig.exclusive_deadline_seconds installer.py:69) and RG-C-016 (lease_acquire_timeout_seconds freshness.py:62). Not a Registry candidate (availability only, no narrowing relation); correct class is host-owned, not retain-as-invariant.

what: Additional sqlite busy-timeout literals not in any crosswalk row: revocation_closeout 10 s, recovery_resolution 10 s, refund_intent 10 s, registry_selection_authority 10 s, authorization_pin _SQLITE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS 2.0

evidence: Source-coverage gap: grep sqlite3.connect shows six timeout literals; crosswalk covers only safe_executor.py:499-501 (W1-054). g_cov check: no row range includes revocation_closeout.py:106, recovery_resolution.py:127, refund_intent.py:113, registry_selection_authority.py:822, authorization_pin.py:117. One logical parameter with six independent sites (count once, per brief); add the sites to NEW:sqlite-busy-timeout.
